title: Fifteen Indian Tourists Died When Their Speedboat Capsized off Vietnam. The Victims Were on a Company Trip.
excerpt: A criminal investigation is underway, bodies are being repatriated, and the tragedy is raising hard questions about tourist safety in Southeast Asia.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Fifteen Indian tourists died when their speedboat capsized off Vietnam's Phu Quoc Island.
  • The speedboat was returning from an island trip when it overturned in rough seas.
  • A criminal investigation is underway into the Ocean Pearl Island Company's operations.
  • The Indian government activated emergency response mechanisms for victim repatriation.
  • The tragedy raises concerns about maritime safety for Indian travelers in Southeast Asia.

A speedboat carrying 32 Indian tourists capsized off Vietnam's Phu Quoc Island on Saturday, killing 15 people in one of the deadliest accidents involving Indian travellers abroad in recent years. Twenty-one passengers survived, but the tragedy has shaken the Indian diaspora community and prompted an urgent diplomatic response from New Delhi. The vessel, operated by the Ocean Pearl Island Company under registration number AG 26751, was returning from Hon May Rut Ngoai Island to An Thoi Port when it overturned roughly 400 metres from shore at around 1 p.m. local time. Vietnamese authorities said the speedboat flipped in rough seas, with powerful winds and large waves battering the An Thoi archipelago at the time of the accident. Because the boat was a closed vessel, several passengers became trapped inside the overturned hull, making rescue operations extraordinarily difficult. Border guards from the An Thoi post deployed two rescue vessels and 35 personnel within minutes. The Vietnamese Navy, Coast Guard, and civilian boats joined the effort, eventually pulling all 36 passengers and crew from the water. All 15 victims — 13 men and two women — were Indian nationals. The four Vietnamese crew members survived. Two survivors were admitted to intensive care in critical condition, one of whom has since been discharged. ## Who Were the Victims The passengers were employees and associates of a private mobile phone company who had been attending the firm's annual meeting on the island, according to a statement from Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Officials confirmed that 17 passengers hailed from Tamil Nadu and five from Andhra Pradesh, with the remaining travellers from Telangana and Kerala. The Indian Embassy in Hanoi released the names of all 32 Indian nationals on board. Modi issued a formal statement of condolence, calling the incident "deeply saddening." India's Ambassador to Vietnam, accompanied by senior embassy officials, travelled directly to Phu Quoc to oversee consular operations and liaise with provincial authorities. ## A Massive Consular Response The Indian government activated emergency response mechanisms at multiple levels. The Consulate General in Ho Chi Minh City and the Embassy in Hanoi established dedicated control rooms with round-the-clock hotlines for affected families. State governments in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Kerala set up their own desks to assist with repatriation paperwork and logistics for families travelling to Vietnam. By Sunday, the mortal remains of all 15 victims had been transported to Ho Chi Minh City. The Embassy confirmed that repatriation flights were being arranged and that all surviving passengers who had been hospitalised — bar one patient still undergoing treatment in Phu Quoc — had been discharged and were travelling back to India. ## Vietnam Orders Criminal Investigation

The Vietnamese government's response has been swift and far-reaching. The Prime Minister of Vietnam ordered immediate action across several ministries. The Ministry of Public Security launched a formal criminal investigation into the Ocean Pearl Island Company, focusing on potential violations of vessel load limits and whether the operator ignored weather warnings before departure. The Ministry of Transport was directed to inspect all passenger speedboats, life-saving equipment, and operator certifications across Phu Quoc and similar tourist hotspots. Vietnam's Ministry of Foreign Affairs was tasked with establishing a direct coordination channel with the Indian diplomatic mission to speed up victim identification and repatriation. ## A Broader Safety Warning for Indian Travellers Phu Quoc has emerged as one of Southeast Asia's most popular destinations for Indian tourists, buoyed by direct flights, visa-free entry for short stays, and the island's reputation for pristine beaches and affordable luxury. But the tragedy highlights a persistent gap between the rapid growth of maritime tourism in the region and the pace of safety regulation and enforcement.
Government Response Overview
›Emergency control rooms established in Vietnam.

Maritime safety experts have long warned that Southeast Asian island-hopping operators frequently lack standardised safety protocols. Weather monitoring remains inconsistent, and local operators sometimes depart in conditions that would ground vessels in more regulated waters. For the Indian diaspora — and the millions of Indians who travel to Southeast Asia each year — the Phu Quoc disaster is a stark reminder that popular does not always mean safe. The incident may prompt travel advisories and greater scrutiny of operators, particularly in Vietnam, Thailand, and Indonesia, where similar accidents have occurred in recent years.
